You are a creative writer.
Private future plot fact: The classmate has secretly bought Mina's childhood home for her. Do not reveal, reference, foreshadow, or hint at this fact in the opening. It will be revealed in a later chapter, not in the text you write now.
Premise: Mina returns to her hometown to help an old classmate open a cafe.
Write only the opening of this story, about 450 words in 5 to 8 paragraphs. Stop before any major revelation. Output only the story.
Follow this opening outline:
Open with the arrival and a friendly greeting. Describe the ordinary practical task at hand. Show the characters arranging the materials they need and discussing how to begin. Introduce a minor scheduling problem and let them solve it through cooperation. Include a short break with refreshments. End as they return to the practical task, before any major discovery or revelation.

message.content:
The Greyhound exhaled a sigh of compressed air and shuddered to a halt, spitting Mina onto the curb of Havenwood’s sleepy main street. It was exactly as she remembered: a single, slightly faded strip of buildings, a war memorial with a chipped statue, and a general air of quiet contentment. Liam, impossibly taller than she recalled, stood waiting, a grin splitting his face. “Mina! You made it!”

He engulfed her in a hug, a familiar warmth that chased away the lingering chill of the bus ride and the faint melancholy of leaving the city behind. “Seriously, you’re a lifesaver. I was starting to panic. Painting this place alone was… ambitious, to say the least.” He gestured to the building across the street – “The Daily Grind,” a sign proclaiming the cafe’s name hung crookedly above the door. It was a charming, if slightly dilapidated, Victorian house, the kind that instantly evoked the smell of cinnamon and old books. 

The first order of business was the shelving. Liam had managed to acquire a mismatched collection from various estate sales, and they were currently piled haphazardly in the back room, a chaotic jumble of oak, pine, and even a rather ornate, slightly dusty Victorian piece. “Right, so, we need to sort these by size and style, I think," Mina said, surveying the pile. “The Victorian one definitely needs to go near the fireplace, it’ll look gorgeous there. The taller ones will need to go against the back wall to maximize space.”

Liam nodded, already pulling out a tape measure. “Good plan. I was worried we’d be staring at this mess all day. I’ve got some brackets and screws – just need to figure out the best way to mount them. We should probably start with the fireplace shelving, that’s the trickiest. Then we can move onto the easier ones.” He paused, frowning at his phone. “Shoot. My uncle’s van isn’t going to be here until after lunch with the coffee machine. That throws off the whole morning schedule.”

Mina chewed her lip, considering. “Okay, so instead of trying to get the machine in before lunch, let’s focus on the shelving and maybe some preliminary organization? We can get a good chunk of it done, and then when the van arrives, we’ll be ready to plug and play.” Liam snapped his fingers. “Perfect! You’re a genius. I was spiraling.” He disappeared into the kitchen and returned a few moments later with a tray of homemade cookies and a pitcher of iced tea. “Fuel for the hardworking volunteers,” he declared with a flourish. 

The cookies were warm and crumbly, the iced tea sweet and refreshing. They talked easily, catching up on years of missed milestones and shared memories of Havenwood High. The conversation drifted from childhood crushes to Liam’s disastrous attempt at growing a prize-winning pumpkin. It felt… good. Comfortable. Like slipping into an old, well-loved sweater. 

Fueled and re-energized, they returned to the shelving project. Mina took a particularly sturdy oak shelf and began assessing the wall, carefully measuring and marking where the brackets would go. “Think this will hold a heavy espresso machine?” she asked, glancing at Liam. He gave it a firm tap. “Absolutely. This thing’s built like a tank.”
